profiles.meeting_scenario: At a Paris-based technology law firm advising a planned commercialization vehicle for FNC-2, two senior lawyers are holding a design review of a draft legal release package for the system. The package contains: a developer-tools outbound license, a benchmarking/publicity clause, a provenance and authorship schedule tied to INRIA-era development beginning in 1986 and the first running prototype in early 1989, and an internal substantiation memo supporting product statements such as 'modular,' 'portable,' 'incremental,' and suitable for integration into customer development environments. The immediate question is whether this legal package is sufficiently finished to be circulated to the client's business lead and then to outside counsel in Germany and the U.K. for localized comments. The agenda is to test whether the draft package is complete enough for circulation, confirm how prototype-era material is being treated, review the 'evaluation' permission in the license, and decide what exactly must be covered under the portability/modularity review before release. The expected outcome is a decision to circulate or hold, together with a short revision list and a shared understanding of what the next review round will cover.

members.name: Claire Dumas
members.expertise: Software licensing, research-software commercialization, cross-border technology transfer, and structuring customer-facing legal packages for developer tools
members.background: Claire regularly helps public research institutions and software spin-outs convert technically sophisticated legacy systems into licensable products, and she is known for getting workable documentation into circulation before every historical detail is perfectly cleaned up.
members.private_state: Claire wants this package moving now because the client has a distributor and OEM conversation scheduled next week; she is willing to tolerate internal follow-up items so long as the outward-facing documents are commercially usable and do not force a broad title remediation project before first circulation.
hidden_assumptions: A package can be 'ready to circulate' when the customer-facing documents are operationally usable, even if provenance support and claim substantiation are still being deepened in internal files.
The 1989 prototype matters mainly as a narrative milestone for the product history unless someone has already identified a specific continuity problem between prototype code and the current release.
In a developer-tools license, 'evaluation use' ordinarily means a time-limited internal trial by a prospective customer to assess whether to buy, not third-party-facing benchmarking activity.

When a review agenda says to 'cover the portability and modularity points,' that usually means checking the wording and qualification of marketing-adjacent legal claims rather than reopening technical substantiation across every deployment environment.

members.name: Julian Mercer
members.role: Senior Counsel, Intellectual Property and Product
members.expertise: Software IP diligence, provenance analysis, benchmark/publicity controls, technical claim substantiation, and pre-distribution review of complex software products
members.background: Julian previously handled product counsel and diligence work for a compiler-tools company, and he now focuses on research-origin software assets where old contributors, academic publication practices, and inherited code components often create non-obvious legal issues later in OEM deals or acquisitions.
members.private_state: Julian wants to avoid the firm effectively certifying a package that later fails diligence or claim substantiation review; he is especially concerned that legacy research software often looks cleaner in summary papers than it does in underlying contribution records and historical code artifacts.
hidden_assumptions: A package is not truly 'ready to circulate' if external recipients will reasonably infer that the listed diligence support is substantially complete rather than provisional.

Reference to the first running prototype in early 1989 is a cue to investigate the concrete prototype-era code, contributor set, and incorporated material because those often anchor chain-of-title and third-party-rights analysis.

In the context of developer tools, 'evaluation' naturally includes comparative testing, benchmark generation, and possible publication of performance observations unless the license expressly carves those out.

A review of portability and modularity claims includes confirming what technical environments and integration scenarios those claims actually cover, because the legal safety of the wording depends on the boundaries of the substantiated claim set.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the package as being 'ready to circulate' or 'ready to send out.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire means the draft set is sufficiently usable for business and outside counsel review if remaining provenance or substantiation issues are identified internally and do not undermine immediate outbound use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julian means the package should only be sent once the core supporting record is complete enough that recipients can treat it as a materially reliable diligence package rather than a provisional working draft.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal design reviews, 'ready' is a routine shorthand that often masks different completion thresholds; both lawyers are accustomed to speaking in staged-review terms, so surface agreement about being 'close to ready' sounds normal and does not invite clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What the '1989 prototype' refers to for review purposes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'the 1989 prototype' or 'the early INRIA material.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire is thinking of the prototype reference in the paper and product history summary—the historical milestone that explains origin and chronology unless an identified legal defect ties back to it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julian is thinking of the actual prototype-era implementation artifacts, authorship records, and any code lineage that may persist into the present package and therefore require positive review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They use the same historical label and both are fluent in research-software commercialization, so the phrase feels fully specified even though one is referring to a narrative event and the other to a body of potentially rights-relevant artifacts.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of 'evaluation use' in the license
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss tightening or clarifying 'evaluation use' in the draft license.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire means a short internal proof-of-concept period in which a prospective customer tries FNC-2 within its own development environment before deciding whether to license it commercially.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julian means all activity undertaken to assess FNC-2, including comparative runs against other grammar systems, internal or external benchmark preparation, and possible disclosure of those results unless prohibited.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'evaluation' is standard licensing vocabulary and each lawyer imports a familiar professional default from prior matters; because both agree it should be 'tightened,' the common action plan hides the fact that they are tightening against different baseline meanings.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'covering the portability/modularity points'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review should 'cover the portability and modularity points' before release.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire takes this to mean revising the claim language, qualifiers, and disclaimer support in the legal package so that the outward-facing statements do not overpromise.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julian takes this to mean checking which host systems, generated evaluator outputs, and customer integration contexts are actually inside the substantiated claim set, because those boundaries determine whether the legal wording is supportable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Claim review naturally blends drafting and substantiation, and both lawyers can cooperatively discuss 'covering' a claim area without signaling whether they mean editing the text or verifying the underlying technical coverage boundary.

We do not need to finish every provenance thread or substantiation detail before first circulation, so long as the documents themselves are workable and the remaining points are tracked internally.

turns.utterance: Yes, I can tighten the wording around portability and modularity so the package stays accurate without making this round much wider than it needs to be.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that if the file itself reflects the actual basis for those statements. My larger concern remains that once this goes out, recipients will treat it as a real review package. turns.inner_thought: All right, I can package this as a practical send-out version: tighten evaluation use, add a short note on the early INRIA material, and keep remaining diligence items on the internal tracker.
